title_en: What are the Aukus submarines actually for? It’s a question the government refuses to answer | Chris Barrie
excerpt_en: Australia should end the Aukus submarine plan and pursue a properly tested strategy to replace the Collins class fleet
body_en: In 1998 I was appointed chief of the Australian defence force. I spent much of my career handling classified information and I understand why some things must stay secret: operational plans, intelligence sources, the capabilities on which lives depend.
But there is a difference between protecting secrets and withholding reasons. On Aukus, Australians have been denied the reasons.

That is the significant lesson I take from serving as a commissioner on the Aukus public inquiry. The government and the opposition declined written invitations to give evidence. No one serving in the Australian Defence Organisation appeared. This means the case for the most expensive defence project in our history – likely to be more than $368bn by the mid-2050s – was never put to us.
Related: We want you! ADF recruitment rates are growing, even as the odds of conflict rise. Why are people signing up?

Instead, we heard from other Australians – young people, their mums and dads, and First Nations Australians – who cannot get straight answers about Aukus and its implications for them. They want to know about the nuclear issues – the waste from the submarine program and the rotation of American and British nuclear-powered submarines through Western Australia, and they want to know about the costs and why Australia is actively supporting submarine building in the US and UK through unconditional financial support.

The government may say it has not been silent. The Australian Submarine Agency has produced fact sheets, a public report and corporate plans. They assert that “only nuclear-powered submarines, acquired through the Aukus partnership, will meet Australia’s defence requirements in the decades ahead”, and that conventional submarines will be “increasingly less able to meet Australia’s needs”. They promise a “strategy of denial” and “impactful projection”. But they do not show the working: which missions, compared with what alternatives, at what cost and with what risk. An assertion is not an explanation.
Let’s start with the simplest question: what are these submarines for?

Nuclear-powered submarines are formidable machines. Their distinctive advantage is speed and endurance underwater, sustainable over long distances, but they are not much good in shallow water. Their characteristics matter most for two missions: hunting other nuclear-powered submarines, including those capable of launching nuclear weapons, and keeping pace underwater with American aircraft carrier battle groups. Conventional submarines can perform most of the other tasks Australia needs.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Impactful projection where, and against whom? If the real purpose is to hunt Chinese submarines near China’s home ports, or to escort American carriers, the government should say so – and explain why these missions serve Australia.

Alone it would be madness for us to take on China. The only plausible way we would be fighting near China’s coast is in a war begun by the United States. Building our future defence force around that possibility is a profound choice, and Australians deserve to have it put to them honestly.

Instead, it looks like this acquisition has become the strategy. We have a recent national defence strategy but there is no national security strategy to show what we are protecting, from what, and how diplomacy, the economy, climate resilience and defence fit together. The United States and the United Kingdom, our partners in Aukus, have published theirs. We should publish ours.
Meanwhile, commitments are being locked in.

From 2027, HMAS Stirling, the navy base near Perth, will host a rotating force of up to four American nuclear-powered submarines and one British. These will not be occasional visits as has been the practice till now. The government has committed up to $8bn to expand the base. Housing is being arranged for American personnel and their families – in a region where people told our inquiry about homelessness on their own doorstep.
Related: Hegseth calls US-built nuclear submarines the ‘apex predator’ of the seas. But are they right for Australia?

Australia has agreed by treaty to take responsibility for disposing of the spent fuel – highly enriched uranium – from its own submarines. The submarine agency’s own corporate plan names its failure to build disposal capability as a key risk, yet it sets no target, timeline or measure for dealing with the waste. Nuclear waste disposal will not be a new conversation for our community but it will be weapons-grade waste – and that is new!

The government says the foreign submarines will be conventionally armed for now – but what about into the future? The US is developing a nuclear-armed cruise missile for its Virginia-class boats. In supporting the Treaty of Rarotonga what conditions will Australia set, and how will they be verified? Could Stirling support nuclear strike operations even if no weapon is stored ashore? Will Stirling become a target for nuclear strike? If so, how will it be protected?
Money already committed is not a reason to commit more. Nor is urgency an excuse to skip strategy.

We have been here before. As a young naval officer, I worked with my bosses on the program to replace the aircraft carrier HMAS Melbourne. The program had been keenly debated for years under the Fraser governments before the Hawke government was elected in 1983. Within two weeks of taking office, it scrapped the carrier program. It then reviewed Australia’s strategic position through a new lens and built a new defence force around contemporary and prospective strategic needs. The Dibb review of 1986 and the 1987 defence white paper are examples of the kind of work we need to do now. It is urgent.

title_en: US tech stocks recover after selloff spooks investors over AI spending
excerpt_en: Midterms didn’t appear to have huge impact, though predicted wins for Democrats could mean more regulation
body_en: US tech stocks made a recovery on Tuesday afternoon after a selloff spooked investors over AI spending.

Tuesday’s midterm elections didn’t appear to have a huge impact on Wall Street, though investors are predicting Democrats get at least a majority in the House and potentially gain seats in the Senate, which could lead to more AI regulation.

The S&P 500 was up 0.37% at market closing on Tuesday, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq increased 0.83% for the day. The Dow dropped 0.38% following a 1.9% dip in Apple’s share price after the company released a worse-than-expected margin forecast due to the higher cost of memory chips.
Nvidia picked up a 2.3% gain after dropping over four sessions, while fellow chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom and Micron Technology also jumped on Tuesday.

Interactive Tuesday marked the end of a brief selloff of AI and tech stocks that started last week, with the Nasdaq in October experiencing its largest monthly decline since March 2025. The Nasdaq had ended on Monday in correction territory, dropping 10% from its 6 October record close.

Small drops in oil prices, amid potential new negotiations with Iran and Russia, also eased investors. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, dropped to $103 a barrel on Tuesday, down from $117 a barrel at the end of October.

While many Americans say frustration with the higher cost of living will be a major factor in their vote on Tuesday, Wall Street has continued to soar off investments in AI, particularly the chips and infrastructure used to power the technology. The S&P 500 is up 10% for the year so far, while the Nasdaq and the Dow are up 9% and 7%, respectively.

Analysis from CNBC of post-midterms market performance from 1980 to 2024 showed the market tends to pick up after an election. Wall Street is often jittery before an election, when results are uncertain, but tends to recover once results are settled.

title_en: Google says there’s no way to use Search without using artificial intelligence
excerpt_en: In announcement geared to schools, tech giant shows how entwined AI is with the world’s most popular website
body_en: Google just acknowledged that you can’t use Google Search without using artificial intelligence.

The search giant announced a slate of new AI products for classrooms and schools on Tuesday as well as more ways for teachers and schools to limit or restrict use of those AI tools. The company said the schools should have control over whether students use AI in the classroom. There’s one catch, though: if a school or teacher blocks the use of Google’s AI features, students won’t be able to use Google Search.

“After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search,” company executives wrote in a blogpost. “Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.”
Related: US teens can access ‘nudify’ apps despite Apple and Google’s parental controls, report finds
In a comment to the New York Times, Chris Phillips, Google’s vice-president for education, said that there is no Google Search without AI.

“Search and AI are deeply integrated,” said Phillips. A school-wide ban on AI would mean that students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available”, he told the Times. The Guardian also reached out to Google but did not hear back by publication.
To some, the move reads like a penalty for not implementing Google’s AI features.

New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, who recently imposed a one-year moratorium on generative AI tools in city schools through the eighth grade, said Google was exploiting its near-total control of online search.

“Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” Mamdani posted on X. “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech.” Lina Khan, former chair of the US Federal Trade Commission, echoed his statement, tweeting that Google was using its monopoly on search to “to coerce schools into adopting AI”.

The ubiquity of Google Search has long made it a critical tool for students, and losing access to it may prove enough of a reason to opt in to using new AI features for schools. Google has also maintained a stranglehold on technology in US classrooms for years by offering cheap and free products. From Gmail and Google Docs to Google Classroom and Google Chromebooks, the company’s suite of software and hardware solutions are among the most widely used in schools.

One of the new features Google announced today was Guided Learning, an AI study tool that “coaches students through the process of problem solving” rather than giving them the answer. The company is planning to integrate Guided Learning directly into Google Search.

“For example, if a student pastes a complex physics problem or asks for help writing a book report in Search, they’ll see prompts to help them think critically and work through the concepts, without going directly to the answer,” the company wrote in a blogpost.

Lila Byock, founder of Schools Beyond Screens, called Google’s announcement a “hostile ultimatum”. Schools Beyond Screens is a national coalition of parents and teachers advocating for more student-centered policies on the use of screens in schools.

“This kind of bullying has no place in our schools,” Byock said in a statement. “Educational value – not shareholder value – must determine which products are used by students and regulators must intervene to prevent big tech from exploiting schoolchildren for profit.”

title_en: Nasa telescope launched in 2004 to plunge back to Earth after failed rescue mission
excerpt_en: Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is expected to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere Wednesday, burning up in the process
body_en: Nasa ’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, which has spent two decades studying the most powerful explosions in the cosmos, is expected to re-enter the Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday, burning up in the process.
The satellite, which was designed to operate with its three telescopes for just two years, is no longer able to steer or observe, and its re-entry is uncontrolled.

The US Space Force predicts the 3,200lb spacecraft will hit the atmosphere at about 3.30am ET on 4 November. Nasa says most of the spacecraft will burn up, but some components are expected to survive.

“Re-entry locations of any surviving components can vary from hemisphere to hemisphere and depend on when it re-enters,” the agency said in a blogpost, adding that surviving fragments are limited between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude.
The agency added: “The risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely – approximately 1 in 2,100. NASA and Space Force will continue to monitor the re-entry and update predictions.”
Related: Japan to launch world-first mission to collect samples from Martian moon
The observatory was launched in 2004 to explore the universe’s most powerful explosions, called cosmic gamma-ray bursts, and quickly return its observations of location and strength to Earth.

Over the course of its operational life, the observatory detected and tracked more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) that are considered the most powerful explosions the universe has seen since the big bang.

Nasa says these bursts of energy occur approximately once per day and are brief, but intense, flashes of gamma radiation and come from all different directions, and can last from a few milliseconds to a few hundred seconds.

But scientists do not know what causes them – theorizing that they may be the birth of a black hole in a massive stellar explosion or produced by the collision of two neutron stars, or some other phenomenon.

Swift was launched as part of Nasa’s medium explorer, or Midex, program. In July, it observed a wandering mega black hole shredding star, which occurs when a star passes fatally close to a supermassive black hole.

“Crumbs of the splintering star heat up as they swirl around the black hole, creating a glow astronomers can see from far across the cosmos, and the black hole launches a relativistic jet into space,” said the agency.

The black hole, described as an “orphan”, lit up as it devoured the star on the outskirts of a galaxy, in what scientists call a “tidal disruption event”. Nearly every galaxy has a supermassive black hole at its center, and a tidal disruption occurs about once every 100,000 years.
The star-shedding event occurred 2,600 light-years from the center of the host galaxy, but the Swift team observed one more than 30,000 light-years away.

“We were looking for these star-shredding events as a way to find otherwise invisible supermassive black holes wandering away from the galactic cores where they usually reside,” said Robert Stein, a research fellow at the University of Maryland, College Park, and Nasa’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, at the time.
Related: SpaceX rocket launch causes stunning ‘jellyfish cloud’ visible off US east coast

A paper describing the results published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, said: “The tidal disruption event outshone its entire host galaxy in ultraviolet wavelengths, temporarily radiating with the light of about 10 billion suns.”

Still unknown is how the black hole came to drift so far. Stein said it could have started off in a small galaxy that merged with the big one, but the key question was how common are wandering black holes.

Nasa attempted to push Swift into a higher orbit last year using a private space contractor but the mission did not succeed after they failed to rendezvous. Last month, Swift was estimated to be orbiting 171 miles above the Earth and it was commanded to end operations to prepare for re-entry.

Nasa said Swift has “broadened our understanding of a wide variety of cosmic objects and events, from active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars undergoing X-ray flares, to supernova explosions and comets and asteroids in our own solar system”.

title_en: How We’re Covering the Midterms — and the Aftermath
excerpt_en: The post How We’re Covering the Midterms — and the Aftermath appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Early voting for the midterms in New York last month Ryan Murphy/AFP via Getty Images This has been a midterm election cycle unlike any other. Wealthy donors spent staggering sums. Both parties moved to redraw congressional district lines. President Donald Trump and his allies relentlessly questioned whether the results could be trusted even before a single ballot was counted. At Trump’s direction, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit that said the federal government would contest any outcome in which Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent in Alaska, was not victorious.

Newsrooms, including ours, have tried to plan how we will cover an election in which the losing side refuses to accept the will of the voters. Was the Alaska lawsuit a single data point or a harbinger?

As we prepare to write about Nov. 3 and beyond, we find ourselves in the uncomfortable position of trying to game out what might happen in the future — not our strong suit. The record shows that journalists are pretty good at telling readers what happened, particularly if we have some time and some data to sift through, and much less good at forecasting the future.

Help Us Report on Key Election Issues ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?

Send Us a Tip And yet we have to plan. Over the past few weeks we have prepared our reporters and editors to cover every scenario we can imagine. None of us have forgotten the chaos of 2020 when Trump was urged by advisers to send the military to seize voting machines in states he had lost. The Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol as lawmakers gathered to certify Joe Biden’s victory underscored the sense that literally anything was possible in the aftermath of elections.

We will have reporters on the ground in 11 key states covering voting, with even more in Washington, D.C., and others on standby. Our reporters have detailed what experts will be watching. But elections are no longer confined to Election Day (early voting and voting by mail constitute a huge share of the electorate). And our plans for covering voting stretch back many months.
Over the past year, we’ve tried to use the techniques of accountability journalism to add new facts to this pivotal moment in American history.

We have focused considerable attention on the mechanics of elections, a once-arcane issue that has become a central aspect of the MAGA movement’s argument that Trump’s 2020 loss was “rigged” by his opponents. We examined how the Trump administration depleted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the arm of the federal government charged with safeguarding election systems. We discovered that Department of Homeland Security officials had asked CISA to obtain a voting machine and hack it without informing the manufacturer of any vulnerabilities found. The plan wasn’t acted on, but its existence made CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. CISA and DHS didn’t respond to our questions, but a White House spokesperson said Trump “has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections.”

Another story looked at how delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures endangered the validity of mail-in ballots in rural counties, typically Republican strongholds, during this year’s primaries. The Postal Service said such delays are less likely in the general election.

One of our most detailed election stories traced the career of Cleta Mitchell, a lawyer who spearheaded the legal attacks on the 2020 results. Mitchell leads a coalition of what she calls “election believers” — people who scour the voting results for errors that they believe point to larger conspiracies. Changes she’d hoped Trump could push through before the midterms, such as compelling states to turn over confidential voter information to the Justice Department, have been blocked by the courts. But she has nonetheless become the voice of a well-funded national movement, one which has the president’s ear. When Trump is weighing what to do in the aftermath of this week’s vote, our reporting strongly suggests that Mitchell will be among the people he listens to.

We asked to speak with Mitchell multiple times. She declined but told us in an email: “What we focus on is making sure the election process is accurate, transparent, and honest. The ONLY steps I’ve urged the Administration to take are those that will give the voters — ALL voters — confidence that the outcomes are correct.” A White House spokesperson said she has no official role in election policy but is an effective private advocate.

We have also spent time doing the traditional work of investigative reporting, looking closely at candidates’ records in public office. A newsroom like ours can’t cover every race, so we focus our resources on areas where we have particular expertise.

Our team in Texas has covered state Attorney General Ken Paxton for years, and we kept our focus once he announced he would run for the U.S. Senate. One story looked at his travels, revealing that only 1 in 6 of his nearly 1,000 out-of-state trips were linked to his official duties. Texas taxpayers paid $3.3 million for Paxton’s security detail to accompany him. (Paxton didn’t answer our questions, but his office said he “faced numerous security threats.”) That has become an issue in the Senate campaign.

title_en: I Was There to Document the Aftermath of Deadly Flooding. Then, It Started Raining.
excerpt_en: The post I Was There to Document the Aftermath of Deadly Flooding. Then, It Started Raining. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: A flash flood along the Rio Ruidoso on July 30, 2025 Three summers ago, over Father’s Day weekend, my family and I went camping in the Lincoln National Forest, just a few hours drive north of our home in El Paso, Texas. It’s a beautiful area that’s long served as a getaway for the region, with skiing in the winter, and golf and hiking in the summer. My daughter played under the trees, and I rode my bike down mountain trails that, I noticed, seemed concerningly dry.

The next evening, after we left to drive home, two fires started in forests surrounding the town of Ruidoso, New Mexico, around 25 miles away from where we’d been. I watched horrifying videos online of fire lapping the mountains behind the village’s strip malls and parking lots. The fires were eventually suppressed by a combination of human effort and the late summer monsoon season. But when the downpour of rain hit the burnt landscape around Ruidoso, it created another problem: Recurring floods then ripped through town, damaging homes and infrastructure, and leading to emergency rescues.

The following summer, the scene repeated. On July 8, 2025, monsoon rain hit a burn scar and quickly swelled the Rio Ruidoso and its tributaries. Three people — two of them children — lost their lives.

Reporter Abe Streep, a member of ProPublica’s Southwest office, and I met in Ruidoso to report on what happened. Ruidoso is a place built on tourism, with a paid (rather than volunteer) fire department staff and its own disaster manager. How could two children and a man be swept to their deaths in a place that appeared equipped to handle such disasters?

In two stories ProPublica recently published, Abe answered those questions. He found that, after the 2024 fires, experts warned the town of increased flash flooding risks. Initially, local and state leaders considered a relocation plan for some homes and businesses that would get people out of harm’s way, but the project faltered. Instead, village leaders continued promoting tourism to the town, and the mayor even chastised residents for warning of floods on social media. Abe also reported that, while local and state officials insisted the emergency response to the flood was admirable, first responders say the three deaths could have been avoided. The responders told Abe that village leadership left them understaffed and inadequately equipped to contend with the flooding.

The Village of Ruidoso did not respond to detailed written questions about its emergency response, and it has not publicly released a report on rescue efforts during the flood. Reached by phone, the fire chief, Cade Hall, disputed our reporting but declined to provide specifics. Mayor Lynn Crawford has said protecting the village includes balancing public safety with tourism, the lifeblood of its economy. But in an interview last year, Crawford said to Abe and me: “Who’s to blame? I didn’t start the fire.”

My role as a photographer was to document Ruidoso as the story unfolded — to visualize the people and place at the center of it. It’s a role I’ve had countless times in my career, but this story hit unexpectedly close to home. I could imagine my own family caught unaware in a similar situation, trying to escape the El Paso summer heat but instead navigating an unfathomable disaster.

A crumbled trailer and debris from flash flooding in Ruidoso on Aug. 1, 2025 The crumbling house at the Riverview RV Park on Sept. 10, 2026 When Abe and I started reporting, we met people from the community and out of town who tried to help. I watched as New Mexico National Guard service members loaded sand bags into families’ cars, people prepared hot meals for those who had been displaced and volunteers handed out donated supplies from collection centers.

Supplies inside a Salvation Army makeshift distribution center and a sandbag distribution point facilitated by the New Mexico National Guard last summer While we were reporting one afternoon, it started raining. Fear swept through me. Our phones lit up with flood warnings from the National Weather Service. We knew we should take them seriously.

Abe and I sought refuge in a local brewery perched high above the river basin. Before we knew it, the water from that thin little creek of Rio Ruidoso became a torrent. The rushing water rose quickly. It swept through the river valley right under the brewery, carrying what looked like trees and debris with it.

A woman watches the Rio Ruidoso rise from inside a brewery in downtown Ruidoso last summer. Two people venture close to the river as a flash flood began to subside last summer. Still, I wanted to photograph the river up close. I left the safety of the brewery and let the heavy rain cover me as I moved closer to the river. As I made photos that afternoon and throughout the rest of the trip, questions about my own safety ran through my mind: Would the water keep rising? If it did, could I get to high ground? And, notably, would I have enough warning?

In hindsight, I realize these questions were largely about whether I could trust the systems in place to keep me and others safe. And as Abe kept reporting over the next year, the more those questions felt valid.

Last month, Abe and I traveled again to Ruidoso. The town felt lighter and less ominous. Much of the ruin had been removed or rebuilt. Grass and sagebrush sprouted on a burn scar. Tourists wandered around a lively downtown on a Friday afternoon. People seemed to be moving on from the terror of the previous year.

title_en: Jon Stewart on Haley Stevens’s betrayal in Michigan: ‘The most diabolical episode of Fargo I’ve ever seen’
excerpt_en: On midterms eve, late-night hosts discussed an 11th-hour endorsement, as Trump focused on his reflecting pool
body_en: On the eve of the US midterm elections, late-night hosts mocked Donald Trump ’s lack of focus on the campaigns, a scandal in the Alaska Senate race and Haley Stevens’s about-face in Michigan.

Jon Stewart With only one day to go until the midterms, “it’s closing arguments time,” said Jon Stewart on Monday evening, “and today, the president took to the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool to make his final case to the voters.”
But instead of talking about the election, Trump instead droned on about his reflecting pool renovations, bragging about “this massive piece of pool”.

“That was the president of the United States, on the day before the midterms, choosing to make a speech at the reflecting pool to talk about the reflecting pool,” the Daily Show host marveled. “No symbolism, no metaphors, just straight-up pool maintenance. That was Donald Trump’s ‘I had it cleaned’ speech, if you will.”

But while Trump’s priorities were, as Stewart put it, “badly misplaced”, Democrats “appear in position for a wave election” in the House and Senate “as long as the remaining couple of days before the election are bombshell-less, drama-free, non-earthquakey”.
Related: Seth Meyers on Trump and Vance’s tactics: ‘No one’s buying your fake folksy bullshit’

And then there’s Michigan, where the Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens switched her endorsement at the 11th hour away from the progressive who defeated her in the primary, Abdul El-Sayed, to the Republican Mike Rogers. “We all knew there was drama in Michigan when Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed defeated Haley Stevens in a contentious primary for the Democratic nomination, but Stevens has always been very clear as to their shared goal of defeating Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers,” said Stewart before several clips of Stevens criticizing Rogers as a “nightmare” Trump Republican who would not stand for Michigan voters.
And yet on Sunday, Stevens posted a video endorsing Rogers seemingly filmed in her car.
“Is her car in a ditch? Is she endorsing Mike Rogers after getting in a car accident?” Stewart wondered. “Real quick, before I lose consciousness, I am endorsing the nightmare.’
“What the fuck happened?” he added. “This is like the most diabolical episode of Fargo I’ve ever seen.

“What could have driven Haley Stevens into the arms of the Rogers campaign?” he asked, before a clip of Stevens alongside Rogers, complaining that she was not invited to any of El-Sayed’s campaign events.

“That says why you’re mad at Abdul. But not why you’re for Rogers,” Stewart said. “Rogers is, hold on, let me find the word, a nightmare, who is against every principle you’ve worked for your entire career.
“I mean, at least say you were visited by three ghosts who convinced you that it turns out people don’t need health insurance,” he added. “This can’t really be about getting your feelings hurt.”

Jimmy Kimmel “More than 57 million Americans have already cast their ballots,” said Jimmy Kimmel on Monday evening. And “Trump made his closing arguments. He chose to do that in front of his ill-fated reflecting pool. What better way to reassure the public that they are in good hands than in front of a pool you’ve repeatedly botched to the tune of $16m?

“Donald Trump, the man who famously promised to ‘drain the swamp’, made his last stand at the site of his own man-made swamp, standing victoriously in front of this hard-won pond like the soldiers who triumphed at Iwo Jima,” he joked.

The president spoke beside the pool for over an hour, and “many are calling it his Pettysburg address,” Kimmel quipped. “He blamed Joe Biden and Obama for everything that happened to the pool before he was there. He said he’s giving serious thought to renaming the pool after himself – which, that’s a nice idea. He ranted about bermuda grass and topsoil and his construction projects and the ballroom, James Comey, rusty pipes. He had visual aids. And then he stripped down to his diapers and did a pretty impressive cannonball into the shallow end of the thing.

“Somehow, the ‘Energizer Dummy’ managed to blabber his way through 30 rallies over the past 32 days,” he added. “And with the campaign for control of Congress at the 2-yard line, Trump is laser-focused on the issues that matter most.”

Seth Meyers In the final stretch until the midterms, “Trump isn’t really hitting the campaign trail,” said Seth Meyers on Late Night. “He’s just kinda falling on it with a big ol’ splat, like a birthday cake hitting the pavement facedown.
“Execution isn’t what he and his buddies are worried about,” he continued. “Don’t focus on the insane things he’s saying. Focus on how hard he’s working and how little he’s sleeping.”
According to Trump, “no president has ever worked so hard on a midterm”, as he’s “working like a dog”.

And yet the president canceled several campaign rallies that were supposed to be held this weekend in Kansas and Iowa. “The dude’s done 30 rallies in less than two months, and suddenly he’s canceling during the final climactic weekend?” Meyers laughed. “That’s like sprinting the first 26 miles of the New York City marathon and then calling an Uber for the last thousand feet.”

Meyers then switched tack to a bombshell New York Times report from the Alaska Senate race. According to the investigation, Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign helped recruit an independent candidate named Dan Sullivan as a spoiler in her race against a different Dan Sullivan.

title_en: Great Britain’s worst-ever bluetongue season ‘a major animal welfare crisis’
excerpt_en: British Veterinary Association president tells MPs surge in cases putting farmers under severe pressure and stress
body_en: The worst bluetongue season on record has been a major animal welfare crisis in Great Britain, MPs have been told, putting farmers under “severe emotional stress”.
Bluetongue, a viral disease that affects sheep, cattle and goats, can cause fever, lesions, stillbirths and death. The tongue may go blue and protrude from the mouth.

The virus, which originated in Africa and is transmitted via biting midges, has spread to Europe over the past two decades, a development the World Organisation for Animal Health links to climate breakdown. The strain of bluetongue currently affecting livestock, serotype 3 (BTV-3), was first found in England in 2023.
The 2025-26 season has been the worst on record. There have been 3,472 cases recorded in England, Scotland and Wales since July, more than five times the past three seasons combined.

Catherine McLaughlin, the chief animal health and welfare adviser at the National Farmers Union, told MPs that this year’s outbreak had placed farmers across the country “under severe emotional pressure and stress”.

“Farmers have faced animal deaths, severe disease, reproductive losses, milk and growth losses, extra labour, veterinary costs, disruption to breeding and sales,” she said. “The emotional turmoil this has placed on farms has been really stark and quite distressing to see.”

The effect of the virus on animal fertility was likely to have long-lasting effects for farms, she said. “We may well be looking at a lot of farms with very low, low numbers of lamb in the spring, which has a massive financial impact on those businesses.”
Dr Gwen Rees, the president of the British Veterinary Association, said because there was no direct treatment for bluetongue, there was little that vets could do.
“You can support those animals and hope they get through it, but that’s a very difficult position to be in for a vet and for a farmer,” she said. “It was a major animal welfare crisis.”
The cost of vaccination and uncertainty about the risk of infection had deterred some farmers from immunising their animals before the outbreak took hold, Rees told MPs.
“Farmers and vets are always balancing risk and benefit and it’s very difficult sometimes to invest in a just-in-case when your margins are extremely tight. The vaccine isn’t a cheap vaccine.”
The worst-hit areas have been in the south-west. Devon has recorded 1,291 cases, Somerset 373 and Cornwall 352.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs defines a case as a premises where at least one animal with bluetongue is present, so the total number of animals affected is likely to be higher than the number of reported cases.

title_en: How different election results affect bank stability – global study
excerpt_en: A study of 22 economies between 2000 and 2023 reveals that elections have a prolonged impact on bank stability.
body_en: Recent elections in Brazil and Israel have yielded different political outcomes. In Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s narrow and ultimately surprise victory in a presidential runoff vote has kept him in office.

In Israel, meanwhile, an inconclusive election result has left uncertainty over the formation of the next government. These outcomes are likely to have an effect on the stability of the financial systems in both countries.

Historically, financial experts believed elections primarily caused brief, nervous jitters in national stock markets. As prior evidence shows, the impact of political uncertainty is often concentrated around the election period, with short-lived spikes in market volatility.
But our 2026 study of 147 national elections across 22 OECD economies between 2000 and 2023 reveals a much deeper, longer-lasting reality.

To understand this, we must first demystify a common banking term: systemic risk. This is the financial equivalent of a domino effect. It is the danger that a shock to one institution or sector could trigger a widespread collapse across the entire financial system.

We saw this in action on a large scale during the 2008 global financial crisis. At that time, the distress of a few highly interconnected institutions threatened to bring down the entire global financial system. Massive government intervention was required to stop the dominoes from falling.

Our findings show that systemic risk follows a broadly hump-shaped trajectory. It dips before scheduled elections, then rises during and after the vote. The risk remains elevated for up to 12 months, particularly when the incumbent government loses office.

Pre-election spending that supports economic activity, alongside possible government suppression of adverse information about economic and financial conditions, offers an explanation for the temporary calm observed before elections.

Systemic risk dips before elections, then rises during and after the vote, remaining elevated for up to 12 months. Kladakis and Skouralis (2026) / Journal of Banking and Finance, CC BY-NC-ND Our study suggests that political continuity can be a financial asset for national banking systems. But Brazil’s recent experience nevertheless shows that continuity does not automatically reassure investors.

Lula reversed a first-round election deficit of more than 2 million votes to secure his reelection. This was the first time since Brazil’s 1985 return to democracy that a president has managed to overturn a first-round defeat.
So the result surprised markets that had positioned for Lula’s challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, to take office.

On October 26, the day after the runoff vote, Brazil’s benchmark stock index fell 13.9%, while its currency lost 8.1% against the US dollar. There was a modest recovery the following day, with stocks gaining around 1%.

The immediate market reaction does not suggest a banking crisis is underway in Brazil. Whether it develops into broader financial instability depends on how financial institutions and borrowers absorb the shock.

Our study also found that elections that yield no clear winner raise systemic risk, as they leave policy uncertainty over budgets and regulation unresolved. Israel has long struggled to establish durable governing coalitions, and its October 27 election left neither main bloc with a parliamentary majority.

While the US president, Donald Trump, had openly endorsed Israel’s incumbent prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, some investors had been positioning for a change of government. The inconclusive result has unsettled markets that had anticipated a clearer political outcome.

During trading on October 28, the day after the election, Israeli stocks fell around 3%. Israel’s currency, the shekel, also weakened by approximately 2% against the US dollar. And the ten-year government bond yield rose nearly five basis points to 4.13%, signalling higher borrowing costs.

Finally, our data shows that snap elections are associated with larger increases in systemic risk. Here, again, Israel is an instructive example. Israel experienced ten elections between 2000 and 2023, seven of which were snap elections. This included five snap elections during its 2018-22 political crisis.
Cushioning the blow Strong economic growth and high public trust in government cushion the financial blow of elections, as they naturally insulate the banking system.

Macroprudential policies, the regulatory guardrails designed to protect the entire banking system, also play a crucial role. By strengthening financial safeguards such as capital buffers for banks, regulators can help the system absorb political shocks.

Unfortunately, evidence suggests that political incentives to stimulate lending before an election can encourage the loosening of these safeguards. This leaves national financial systems more exposed to subsequent shocks.
In Turkey and India, for example, governments have historically used state-owned banks to expand consumer and mortgage credit aggressively before tightly contested elections.

This creates a short-term boost in economic activity and voter goodwill, but often leaves the financial system vulnerable to a hangover of non-performing loans and instability once the votes are counted.

title_en: Booker prize 2026: a diverse list to inspire all sorts of readers – six experts review the nominees
excerpt_en: There’s comedy, there’s politics, there’s history, there’s queerness and there’s drama. The 2026 shortlist is packed full of goodness.
body_en: When the Booker prize was first launched in 1969, its aim was to get more people reading and to stimulate discussion about contemporary literature. Now, we all know reading is at an all time low but there really has never been a better time to reignite your love of fiction and to discover (or rediscover) your love of reading. And, this year’s shortlist is really a testament to the breadth of stories available out there.

There’s poetic historic fiction with May we Feed the King about a reluctant medieval king from Rebecca Perry. For lovers of science fiction, M. John Harrison has written a tale about aliens and social collapse set on the Kentish coast. And, there’s laughter to be found in Black Bag by Luke Kennard about an out-of-work actor who lands a gig in a psychological experiment.

There are also new works by previous winners and nominees. Marlon James is back with a startling portrait of the lives of gay men in Jamaica. Douglas Stuart gives us his chilly Hebridean family drama, John of John. And, finally there’s the gentle political commentary of Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say about what happens when good people stay quiet.
Ahead of the prize being announced on November 9, we’ve asked six experts to guide you through the nominations for 2026.

Black Bag by Luke Kennard Black Bag was inspired by a 1967 experiment at Oregon State University in which an individual cloaked in black sat mutely in a seminar for a semester. Where the study focused on the reactions of the witnesses, Black Bag is the story and meditations of the man who becomes increasingly attached to his role and, amusingly, his bag.

Kennard’s protagonist is a flat-broke actor relying on cash-in-hand corporate murder mysteries and the kindness of his friend Claudio in an otherwise dismal world. Wearing the bag outside of the classroom not only removes the problem of how to be but even attracts the attention of a female professor who wants “to fuck nothing” – he is both strikingly visible and anonymous. The novel is laugh-out-loud funny but melancholy and provocative too. Some of Bag’s strongest relationships are those he imagines, like ongoing conversations with his parents’ dog and narrated village life with a fictional Swedish wife.
By Tory Young, associate professor in English literature

The End of Everything by M. John Harrison The backdrop of The End of Everything is alien invasion, but treated with a ludic contempt for genre conventions. An ineffectual war is being waged against the sardonically named iGhetti – amorphous entities who have leaked into the world “from the astral plane”. Phillip Tennent, a beachcomber somewhere on the Kent coast, finds an iGhetti artefact washed up by the tide, a thing that slowly begins to ape humanity, an event which throws Tennent’s life and the life of his ageing, forgetful aunt, Marnie, into brutality and random violence.

In his 2023 “anti-memoir”, Wish I Was Here, M. John Harrison writes of his world-building: “I’d rather pile up real facts to reveal something evidently unreal than pile up invented facts to make something unreal seem real.” The real facts pile up here – cheek by jowl with dense allusion and the surreal – into a work of slippery unreality, which is nevertheless congested with raw feeling and startling poetry.
Tim Jarvis, senior lecturer in creative writing

The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout Elizabeth Strout’s slight book is a series of snapshot insights into the thoughts and memories of protagonist, Massachusetts Bay high school History teacher Artie Dam. With Artie at the centre, it captures the problems, relationships, and futures of a community: extended family, students, colleagues, whose lives connect unexpectedly, or are influenced by brief interactions – statements of support or honesty. Sometimes, Artie worries he lies through kindness; he isn’t to know that his positivity manifests unexpected joys.
Nominated for the prize three times before, Pulitzer-winner Strout’s elegant text is both melancholic and evocative.

Measured, thoughtful, and good, Artie Dam is caught up in political, socioeconomic, personal, and philosophical questions threatening to derail his life. These also bring him closer to people he loves, including his son Rob and his extravagant, reckless friend, Flossie. Artie clings on to the possibility of free will while the reader hopes that everything will work out well for Artie.
Jenni Ramone, associate professor of postcolonial and global literature

The Disappearers by Marlon James The Disappearers pulls the reader into a seemingly knowable time and place – the Jamaica of 1988 to 2005. Yet what James seeks to make known and felt is not to be found in any record or archive.

The action begins as eight men gather to rehearse John Herbert’s provocative and unsettling 1967 US prison play Fortune and Men’s Eyes about homosexuality and sexual power play. A homophobic mob storms a rehearsal and by the end of the evening, one man is murdered and another blinded. Shortly afterwards, two disappear. Six years later, the search for the disappeared continues and the novel makes it clear that gay men in Jamaica disappear way before anyone notices they’ve gone.

In Marlon’s writing of their differences in class, ethnicity, social privilege, sexual preference, desire for attachment, emotional intelligence, eloquence, and identity constructions, the novel writes away the enforced flatness of slurs and stereotypes of gay men to humanise at scale. It’s an everyday act of narrative restitution that has revolutionary significance given the continuing sexual politics of Jamaica.

title_en: Who mapped Africa? Debunking the myth that Europeans alone plotted the continent
excerpt_en: African guides drew lines in the sand to help Europeans understand the terrain. But they rarely got the credit.
body_en: An 1805 European map depicting the mythical Mountains of Kong range. Wikimedia Commons After the United Nations adopted a resolution in September 2026 endorsing a map that more fairly represents the size of Earth’s landmasses, author and journalist Moky Makura of Africa No Filter – a main sponsor of the Correct the Map initiative – asked: “What else about Africa is the world underestimating that’s also hidden in plain sight?”

The initiative brought attention to the way continents are distorted by projections that display our rotund planet on two-dimensional maps, something that has long made Africa especially appear far smaller than it actually is. But it left another assumption untouched: that European maps of Africa – which became the basis of how we see African countries today – are based solely on the observations of the Europeans who made them.

As an expert on the map history of Africa, I know that this is a misconception which deserves rethinking. Recent research by myself and others on colonial-era mapping of West Africa demonstrates that much of the geographical information these maps show is based on African observations. It’s just that Europeans largely took the credit.

A line in the sand Most African map traditions are undocumented or ephemeral. But ground and oral mapping was common in the pre-colonial period, and often highly valued. European explorers relied upon these indigenous mapping practices during their travels and sometimes incorporated them into their own maps.

For example, sections of French explorer Henri Duveyrier’s 1861 map of the Sahara owed much to the maps drawn in the sand by his guide, Cheikh‐‘Othmàn. Indeed, more than a third of Duveyrier’s map is based on information provided by local sources.

Part of Henri Duveyrier’s and Edouard de Desbuisson’s 1861 map of the western Sahara showing African-sourced routes in solid black lines and European-surveyed routes in solid red lines. Bibliothèque nationale de France A common objective of mapping is to solve a spatial problem. Route mapping is all about finding one’s way between points A and B and determining the distances between them. For Europeans, it was important to know where African leaders resided or the most direct route to important trade centers.

When European explorers and soldier-surveyors inquired, African guides, interpreters and merchants described the road ahead and often drew these routes on the ground with a stick. Europeans valued African oral and ground-mapping practices for their contributions to knowledge; they were also useful for empire building.

In his 1892 travel memoir, French Navy Lt. Louis-Gustave Binger reproduced the plan of Niellé, a city in contemporary northern Ivory Coast that was drawn on the ground by his interpreter, Fofana Diawé.

African guides and interpreters, Fofana Diawé and Moussa Diawara, contributed to Lt. Louis-Gustave Binger’s 1887-1889 exploration and mapping of the Niger River Bend region of West Africa. Binger/Du Niger au Golfe de Guinée par le pays de Kong et le Mossi Niellé’s chief prohibited Binger from visiting the town, making Diawé’s drawing particularly valuable. In another instance, Binger reports that an African intermediary placed varied lengths of straw on the ground to indicate the distances between localities in the Kong region.

In his exploration of the area between the Niger River and the Gulf of Guinea in the early 1890s, Navy Lt. Jean-Baptiste Marchand routinely collected route information from local inhabitants about places he could not visit. This “locally sourced route information,” as he described it, appears as dashed lines on his landmark map of the region. The routes of Marchand and other European explorers appear as solid lines.

African guide and interpreter Fofana Diawé’s ground map of Niellé reproduced by French Navy Lt. Louis-Gustave Binger. Binger, 1882 When the total distance of all routes is calculated, African sources account for 65% of routes on Marchand’s map.
Thanks to African intermediaries guiding these military explorers, Binger discovered that the fabled Kong Mountains, which stretched across most 19th-century maps, did not exist.

And Marchand learned that the savanna penetrated more deeply into the rainforest in south-central Ivory Coast. The elimination of the imaginary Kong Mountains and knowledge of a shorter travel distance through the dense tropical forest accelerated French colonization of the region.

But this practice of displaying locally sourced route information on European maps was debated among European geographers and military officers. Some mapmakers refused to display African mapping because it did not follow the standards of scientific cartography.

They argued that the geographical information was based on hearsay rather than measurement. Others, particularly military officers trying to expand colonial boundaries, appreciated locally made maps’ practical value. Embedded in this debate was the self-claimed civilizing mission ideology underpinning colonialism, which assumed the superiority of European knowledge. The dashed lines suggest that locally sourced information was tentative and would eventually be replaced by solid lines based on European measurements.

A digitized version of Jean-Baptiste Marchand’s 1896 map of part of West Africa. Locally sourced route information is shown in blue dashed lines. Afriterra – The Cartographic Free Library. Filling in the blanks The appearance of blank spaces on maps is typically seen as demonstrating the scientific standard of accuracy: Cartographers don’t show what we don’t know.
Blank spaces were also viewed as instrumental to imperial expansion. That’s because they suggested vacant areas open to colonization.

The common denominator of both views is that Europeans determine what is shown and not shown on maps of Africa. But a closer look at explorers’ and soldier-surveyors’ reports indicates that blank spaces often emerged from the refusal of African authorities to allow Europeans to travel through their territory.

title_en: This Oil Company Is Linked to 1,000 Pollution Incidents and Other Violations. Oklahoma Never Punished It.
excerpt_en: The post This Oil Company Is Linked to 1,000 Pollution Incidents and Other Violations. Oklahoma Never Punished It. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Photo illustration by Jovelle Tamayo/ProPublica. Source images: Nick Oxford for ProPublica, courtesy of Mike Faulkner, and obtained in an open records request from the Oklahoma Corporation Commission. In June 2023, staff at an Oklahoma regulatory agency were fed up. The state isn’t known for cracking down on oil and gas companies for polluting the environment, but for over a year, the staff had been building a case to punish Citation Oil & Gas, one of the nation’s largest privately owned oil companies.

About 30 miles north of the Texas border, toxic wastewater was gushing from the ground outside the small city of Ardmore. In the mile-wide oil field known as the Bayou, an oily sheen glistened on creeks and long streaks of salt scarred the land. The so-called purges, bubbling up among stands of oak and walnut trees, also threatened drinking water sources, drawing attention from the Environmental Protection Agency, according to a federal report.

State investigators pinned the blame on Citation’s injection wells, which pump wastewater from oil production back underground at high pressures and volumes in order to produce more oil. But this injection came with risks.

Days earlier, the agency had asked Citation to cut injection pressures in half. The company refused, prompting staff at the oil division of the Oklahoma Corporation Commission, the state’s oil and gas regulator, to recommend an official punishment through the agency’s court system.
“This will be an important case to get some of these purges stopped and particularly concerning Citation’s operations,” Danny Ray, an agency manager at the time, emailed his colleagues.
He restated the urgency three days later in an email to oil division leaders and Citation officials: “We consider this an emergency situation that needs to be addressed promptly.”

A salt scar in a southern Oklahoma oil field known as the Bayou in 2022 Obtained in an open records request from the Oklahoma Corporation Commission An old well releases a stream of wastewater in the Bayou in 2022. Obtained in an open records request from the Oklahoma Corporation Commission To stop the flow of wastewater, the agency temporarily shut down the Bayou’s 22 injection wells — all but three of which were owned by Citation — kicking off a yearlong fight over the terms under which injection could restart.
Under state rules, companies must not pollute, and oil and gas regulators at the Corporation Commission can revoke injection permits and issue fines to those that violate regulations.

But agency leadership ultimately did not follow staff guidance to punish Citation through the commission’s administrative law court. Instead, in April 2024, state officials, including the oil division’s then-Director Robyn Strickland, would allow Citation to restart injection at higher-than-recommended pressures.

Agency leaders’ reluctance to punish Citation reflects a longstanding pattern of Oklahoma regulators letting oil companies contaminate drinking water, farmland and people’s homes with scant consequences, The Frontier and ProPublica have found in a yearlong investigation.

In fact the commission has no record of ever fining or completing an enforcement case against Citation, the company named more than any other in the agency’s database of pollution reports and other rule violations, listed more than 1,000 times over the past decade. That’s hundreds more incidents than any other operator, including comparably sized companies. In recent years, purges linked to Citation include some of Oklahoma’s longest, most damaging oil field pollution events.

Current and former employees at the Oklahoma Corporation Commission describe top agency officials as wary of going after habitual violators like Citation. Citation has become Oklahoma’s second-largest well owner after taking over collections of aging, low-producing wells from oil giants that have largely left the state for more lucrative oil fields in Texas and elsewhere; the company acquired its Bayou wells in 2010. Regulators treat Citation gently, current and former agency employees say, because the company holds onto aging wells that are worth little — wells that could easily become a financial liability for the state if Citation were to sell or walk away from them.

A spokesperson for the Oklahoma Corporation Commission declined to answer questions about the regulatory agency’s handling of Citation’s record, noting the possibility of future enforcement actions or litigation involving the company.

“The OCC Oil and Gas Conservation Division must remain mindful of its regulatory and adjudicatory responsibilities and avoid making public statements that could potentially affect future proceedings or legal considerations,” spokesperson Jack Damrill said in an email.

Strickland has since left the agency for a job as chief projects officer for the Interstate Oil and Gas Compact Commission, a quasi-governmental organization that often advocates for industry interests. She did not respond to requests for comment.
A Citation executive declined to comment in response to written questions.

Regulators in other jurisdictions have at times come down hard on Citation, which owns wells in 11 other states. In 2017, the company settled with the U.S. Department of Justice for $2.25 million over allegations of underpaid royalties from drilling on federal land in Wyoming, though the settlement did not rule that the company was liable in the case. And in 2025, Utah reached a $700,000 settlement with the company after a crude oil and wastewater spill. Texas and Colorado have also fined Citation in recent years for violations.

“Citation has been the thorn in my side for a long time,” said a current manager at the Oklahoma agency who spoke on the condition of anonymity to protect their job. “They just operate however they want. They’ve had major pollution issues, and you can’t really touch them.”
